title: The 50/72 Rule — Writing Clear Commit Subject Lines

checkpoint_1.q1_50_char_rationale: Correctly identified git log --oneline truncation and the 'doing too much' signal. Missed the 50/72 two-tier distinction and GitHub display contexts.
checkpoint_1.q2_subject_line_exercise: Strong: correct type (feat), scope (tasks), imperative mood, length (38 chars), no trailing period. Initially lowercase — pushed back on capitalization correction (correctly).
checkpoint_1.hands_on_rewrites: All five rewrites demonstrated solid command of rules. Notable: #5 (wip) correctly identified as structurally wrong rather than just badly worded — strong conceptual insight. #1 slightly awkward verb choice ('obscure' vs 'mask'). #4 cleanest fix of the set.

key_takeaways: 50 chars is the target for the entire subject line; 72 is the hard ceiling before truncation
Imperative mood: 'add', not 'added' or 'adding' — use 'if applied' test to verify
No trailing period — subject lines are titles, not sentences
Be specific enough that the reader can reconstruct what changed without opening the commit
WIP commits are structurally wrong, not just badly named
Capitalization after the CC prefix is a project-level style choice, not a spec requirement
helm_deliverable: Rewrote 5 vague Helm commit subject lines applying 50/72 rule, imperative mood, and specificity standards
objectives_met: Apply the 50-character subject line limit and explain why it matters
Write commit subjects in imperative mood correctly and consistently
Identify and fix vague or over-broad commit descriptions
Distinguish good from bad subject lines at a glance
misconceptions_noted: Initial answer on Q1 did not distinguish 50 (target) from 72 (hard cap) — treated 50 as a single cutoff rather than a two-tier constraint
professor_notes: Strong performance consistent with expert-level conventional_commits baseline. This is a pattern of quality-control engagement that appeared in L01 (caught checkpoint count mismatch) and continues here.
